clinicalPearls: A heterogeneous group of disorders united by punctate epiphyseal and cartilage calcification (stippling) on radiographs.

Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata is a peroxisomal disorder of plasmalogen synthesis (PEX7, GNPAT, AGPS) with proximal limb shortening, cataracts, profound developmental delay, seizures and coronal vertebral clefts.

The X-linked dominant form (Conradi-Hünermann-Happle, EBP encoding sterol delta-8-delta-7 isomerase) affects females with asymmetric limb shortening, ichthyosis following the lines of Blaschko, cataracts and patchy scarring alopecia, and is usually lethal in males.
The X-linked recessive brachytelephalangic form (CDPX1, arylsulfatase E) shows nasomaxillary hypoplasia, a depressed nasal bridge and short distal phalanges.
Important non-genetic phenocopies include maternal warfarin embryopathy, maternal autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus, and vitamin K deficiency.
Cataracts are common across subtypes, so early ophthalmology review is essential.
The radiographic stippling regresses with age and is replaced by epiphyseal dysplasia, so a later normal film does not exclude the diagnosis.
Cervical spine stenosis or instability can complicate several subtypes.
reference.pathophysiology: Chondrodysplasia punctata is a radiographic phenotype produced by several distinct disturbances of cartilage matrix mineralisation and endochondral ossification. In the rhizomelic forms, defective peroxisomal function, through the PTS2 import receptor PEX7 or the plasmalogen-synthesising enzymes encoded by GNPAT and AGPS, causes plasmalogen deficiency and impaired phytanic acid oxidation. The X-linked dominant Conradi-Hünermann-Happle form arises from mutations in EBP encoding sterol delta-8-delta-7 isomerase, leading to accumulation of cholesterol precursors, with X-inactivation explaining the mosaic, Blaschko-linear skin changes and asymmetric skeletal involvement. The X-linked recessive brachytelephalangic form reflects arylsulfatase E deficiency. Several phenocopies share disruption of the vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of matrix proteins such as matrix Gla protein and osteocalcin, which is why maternal warfarin exposure and vitamin K deficiency can reproduce the picture.
additionalDifferentials: Zellweger spectrum and other peroxisomal biogenesis disorders
Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome and other inborn errors of cholesterol synthesis
Warfarin embryopathy and maternal vitamin K deficiency
Maternal systemic lupus erythematosus or other autoimmune disease
Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia and Morquio syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey to document the distribution of stippling and limb shortening
Red-cell plasmalogens with plasma very-long-chain fatty acids and phytanic acid for peroxisomal disease
Plasma sterol profile for accumulation of cholesterol-synthesis intermediates
Targeted molecular genetic testing (PEX7, GNPAT, AGPS, EBP, ARSE)
Maternal history and autoantibody screen where a phenocopy is suspected
redFlags: Progressive respiratory compromise or feeding difficulty in infants with the rhizomelic form
Signs of cervical cord compression from spinal stenosis or instability
Dense bilateral cataracts threatening irreversible amblyopia
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends entirely on subtype: the rhizomelic form is severe, with most affected children dying in early childhood, whereas the brachytelephalangic and many X-linked dominant cases are compatible with normal cognition and lifespan, the main issues being orthopaedic, dermatological and ophthalmological.
pitfalls: Assuming a single cause for the stippling rather than working systematically through the differential
Missing a maternal warfarin exposure or maternal autoimmune disease as the underlying explanation
Failing to identify the peroxisomal rhizomelic form, which requires specific metabolic testing and genetic counselling
Falsely reassuring on the basis of a later radiograph taken after the stippling has resolved
